items.prose: Open intervals generate the Borel sets. Closed and half-open intervals, points and countable sets all need a short argument.
items.question: Select all that apply. Which of these sets are Borel?

options.text: The set of $x \in [0, 1]$ with no digit 7 in its decimal expansion
The rationals with denominator a power of 2

options.why: You included $V$. It is the standard example of a set with no length, so it is not Borel.
You included every subset. The Vitali set is a subset that is not Borel.

feedback.correct: The half-open interval, the no-7 set and the dyadic rationals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build each set from intervals by countable unions, intersections and complements.

explain.text: $[0.2, 0.7) = \bigcup_n [0.2, 0.7 - \tfrac1n]$ is a countable union of closed intervals. The no-7 set is a countable intersection of finite unions of intervals. The dyadic rationals are a countable union of points, and a Vitali set is not Borel.

items.prose: The Cantor construction keeps $(2/3)^n$ of the length at stage $n$, in $2^n$ intervals.

parts.question: At which stage does the remaining length first fall below 0.001?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $n$ with $(2/3)^n < 0.001$.

byKey.seventeen: At stage 17 the length is 0.001015, still just above 0.001.

parts.question: How many intervals are there at that stage?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each stage doubles the number of intervals.

byKey.half: That is $2^{17}$, the count at stage 17.

explain.text: Each stage splits every interval into two, so stage 18 has $2^{18} = 262{,}144$ intervals.

parts.question: The end points of all the removed intervals form a set $E$. Is $E$ countable?

options.text: Yes. Each stage adds finitely many, so they can be listed stage by stage.
No. Every point of the Cantor set is an end point, so $E$ is uncountable.
options.why: You treated $E$ as the whole Cantor set. Points such as $\tfrac14$ are in the Cantor set but are not end points.

options.text: No. Each stage adds more end points than the last, so the count has no limit.
options.why: You saw the counts grow. Each stage adds finitely many, and a countable union of finite sets is countable.

feedback.correct: Countable: the end points can be listed stage by stage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the end points that each stage adds.

explain.text: Stage $n$ removes $2^{n-1}$ intervals, so it adds $2^n$ end points. List stage 1, then stage 2, and so on. Every end point of a removed interval appears, so $E$ is countable.

items.prose: A strategy breaches a risk limit on day $k$ with chance $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$. We know nothing about how the days relate.
items.question: Use the union bound to cap the chance of any breach from day 100 on. Give 5 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ for every $k \ge 100$ and compare with an integral.

byKey.telescope: That is the cruder bound $\tfrac{1}{99}$ from $\tfrac{1}{k^2} \le \tfrac{1}{k(k-1)}$. The sharper value is 0.01005.
byKey.first: You gave the chance on day 100 alone, $\tfrac{1}{100^2}$.

explain.text: $\sum_{k \ge 100} \tfrac{1}{k^2}$ is close to $\int_{99.5}^{\infty} x^{-2}\,dx = \tfrac{1}{99.5} = 0.01005$. The exact value is $\tfrac{\pi^2}{6} - \sum_{k<100} k^{-2} = 0.0100502$.

items.prose: Let $A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ with $A = \bigcap_n A_n$ and $P(A_1) < \infty$. We prove continuity from above using continuity from below. Two lines are flawed.
items.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $C_n = A_1 \setminus A_n$. The $C_n$ increase, because the $A_n$ decrease.
$\bigcup_n C_n = A_1 \setminus A$, because a point leaves some $A_n$ exactly when it is outside $\bigcap_n A_n$.
By continuity from below, $P(C_n) \to P(A_1 \setminus A)$.
By finite additivity, $P(C_n) = P(A_1) - P(A_n)$ and $P(A_1 \setminus A) = P(A_1) - P(A)$, both finite because $P(A_1) < \infty$.
So $P(A_1) - P(A_n) \to P(A_1) - P(A)$, and subtracting the finite $P(A_1)$ gives $P(A_n) \to P(A)$. $\blacksquare$
The sets $C_n = A_1 \setminus A_n$ decrease, so continuity from above applies to them.
lines.why: You said the $C_n$ decrease. They increase, and using continuity from above would assume what we are proving.

lines.text: $P(A_1 \setminus A_n) = P(A_1) - P(A_n)$ holds even if $P(A_1) = \infty$.
lines.why: You allowed an infinite $P(A_1)$. Then $\infty - \infty$ has no value, and the formula fails.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuity from above follows from continuity from below plus finiteness.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sets $C_n$ are built first, then continuity from below is used.

byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: The complements $C_n$ increase to $A_1 \setminus A$, so continuity from below applies. Finiteness of $P(A_1)$ lets us subtract. That is why the theorem needs $P(A_1) < \infty$.

items.prose: Let $U$ be uniform on $(0, 1)$, let $r > 0$, and let $X = -\tfrac{\ln U}{r}$. For $x > 0$, $\{X \le x\}$ is an event about $U$.
items.question: Write $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$ in terms of $r$ and $x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $X \le x$ into a statement about $U$.

byKey.surv: You gave $P(X > x) = P(U < e^{-rx})$. The distribution function is one minus that.

explain.text: $X \le x$ means $-\ln U \le rx$, that is $U \ge e^{-rx}$. The uniform chance of that is $1 - e^{-rx}$, so $X$ is exponential with rate $r$.

items.prose: Three tosses give $\Omega = \{HHH, \dots, TTT\}$. The events are "first toss heads" and "at least two heads". Outcomes with the same membership in every event cannot be told apart: they form an atom.

items.title: The first Borel-Cantelli lemma
items.prompt:
Let $A_1, A_2, \dots$ be events with $\sum_n P(A_n) < \infty$.

1. Prove that $P(A_n \text{ infinitely often}) = 0$. Write the event as $\bigcap_n \bigcup_{k \ge n} A_k$, bound with the union bound, and pass to the limit by continuity from above.
2. A strategy breaches a limit on day $n$ with chance $\tfrac{1}{n^2}$. What follows about the number of breaches, and what is the bound on any breach from day 50 on?
items.model:
**The event.** An outcome lies in $A_k$ for infinitely many $k$ when it never stops appearing. That is: for every $n$, it lies in some $A_k$ with $k \ge n$. So $\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\} = \bigcap_n B_n$ with $B_n = \bigcup_{k \ge n} A_k$.

**Decreasing sets.** The $B_n$ decrease, since $B_{n+1} \subseteq B_n$, and $P(B_1) \le 1 < \infty$.

**The union bound.** By countable subadditivity, $P(B_n) \le \sum_{k \ge n} P(A_k)$. The right side is the tail of a convergent series, so it tends to 0 as $n \to \infty$. Hence $P(B_n) \to 0$.

**Continuity from above.** The $B_n$ decrease and $P(B_1) < \infty$, so $P(\bigcap_n B_n) = \lim_n P(B_n) = 0$. Therefore $P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 0$. $\blacksquare$

**The strategy.** $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6 < \infty$, so with chance 1 the strategy breaches only finitely often, whatever the dependence between days. The chance of any breach from day 50 on is at most $\sum_{k \ge 50} 1/k^2 \approx 0.0202$, because $P(B_{50}) \le \sum_{k \ge 50} P(A_k)$.

rubric.text: Writes $\{A_n \text{ i.o.}\} = \bigcap_n \bigcup_{k \ge n} A_k$ and gives the reason: in infinitely many $A_k$ means beyond every $n$ in some $A_k$
Names $B_n = \bigcup_{k \ge n} A_k$ as a decreasing sequence with $P(B_1)$ finite, so continuity from above is allowed
Bounds $P(B_n) \le \sum_{k \ge n} P(A_k)$ by the union bound (countable subadditivity)
Says the tail of a convergent series tends to 0, so $P(B_n) \to 0$
Concludes $P(\bigcap_n B_n) = \lim P(B_n) = 0$ by continuity from above
Applies it: $\sum 1/n^2 < \infty$ gives finitely many breaches almost surely, and a bound about 0.0202 from day 50 on
